5200:
An en dash is a punctuation mark — a small horizontal line — that sits between two things to show a connection, a range, or a relationship between them. It looks like this: –

It has a specific job in writing: to link things that belong together as a pair or a span.
How It Looks Compared to Similar Marks

There are three horizontal-line marks in English writing, and confusing them is extremely common. Here they are side by side:

  • Hyphen → - (the shortest; found on your keyboard)
  • En dash → – (medium length)
  • Em dash → — (the longest)

The en dash gets its name from typography: it is traditionally the same width as the capital letter N. The em dash is the width of M. These are just naming conventions — what matters is what each mark does, not its width.
What the En Dash Does: Its Core Meaning
The en dash means "through," "to," or "between." It connects two endpoints of a range, or shows that two things are linked as equal partners or opposites.
Use 1: Showing a Range of Numbers, Dates, or Times

This is the most common and straightforward use. When you have a start point and an end point — numbers, dates, pages, times — you use an en dash to connect them.

  • Pages 45–78 (meaning: from page 45 to page 78)
  • The years 1990–2005 (from 1990 to 2005)
  • 9:00 AM–5:00 PM (from 9 AM to 5 PM)
  • Chapters 3–7 (chapters 3 through 7)
  • Ages 8–12 (for children aged 8 to 12)

Notice there are no spaces around the en dash when used this way. It sits snugly between the two values.

Important rule: When you write "from X to Y" or "between X and Y" in full words, you do not use an en dash. The en dash replaces the words "to" or "through." So you would not write "from 1990–2005" — that would be redundant. You'd write either "from 1990 to 2005" (all words) or "1990–2005" (en dash only).
Use 2: Connecting Two Places, Names, or Concepts That Are Equal Partners

When two separate things — cities, people, ideas — are paired as equals, the en dash shows that connection. Think of it as saying "and" or "versus" or "between" in a compressed form.

  • The New York–London flight (a flight that connects New York and London as two equal endpoints)
  • A Democrat–Republican debate (a debate between two opposing sides)
  • A supply–demand problem (the tension between supply and demand)
  • A parent–child relationship (connecting two roles)
  • The Brazil–Argentina match (two teams facing each other)

A hyphen would be wrong here because a hyphen is for gluing parts of a single word together (like "well-known" or "blue-green"). An en dash is for connecting two distinct and separate things.
Use 3: Compound Modifiers With a Multi-Word Part

This one is a bit more subtle but important. In English, when you describe a noun using multiple words together (a compound modifier), you normally use a hyphen: a "well-known author," a "fast-moving train."

But what happens when one of the parts is itself made of two words, or is a proper name (like a place or a title)? A hyphen would be awkward or unclear — it would look like it's just connecting individual words rather than showing the full grouping. That's when you use an en dash instead.

  • A Nobel Prize–winning author (the modifier is "Nobel Prize–winning" — "Nobel Prize" is a two-word phrase acting as one unit)
  • A New York–based company (based in New York, where "New York" is a two-word proper noun)
  • Post–World War II architecture (architecture from after World War II; "World War II" is a multi-word name)
  • A climate change–related policy (related to climate change)
  • A left-wing–leaning newspaper (here "left-wing" is already a hyphenated compound, so an en dash elevates the whole thing)

The logic is: when any part of a compound modifier contains more than one word, upgrade from a hyphen to an en dash to show that those words form a single unit.
Use 4: Scores and Votes

En dashes appear naturally in scores, vote counts, and results to show the split between two sides.

  • The team won 3–1.
  • The vote passed 7–3.
  • The score was 110–98.
How the En Dash Differs from the Hyphen

The hyphen (-) is for:

  • Joining parts of a compound word: mother-in-law, well-being, twenty-one
  • Joining a prefix to a word: pre-war, self-aware
  • Breaking a word at the end of a line in print

The en dash (–) is for:

  • Ranges (numbers, dates, times)
  • Equal pairings of separate things
  • Compound modifiers with multi-word parts

The key distinction: a hyphen binds parts of a single word. An en dash links two separate, independent things.
How the En Dash Differs from the Em Dash

The em dash (—) is used for a completely different purpose. It creates a dramatic pause or break inside a sentence, sets off a side comment, or signals an interruption. It works at the level of sentences and clauses, not at the level of words and ranges.

  • She finally told him the truth — and he was devastated.
  • The answer — if there even is one — won't come easily.

The en dash works at the word or phrase level, quietly linking ranges and paired concepts. It's more subtle and clinical. The em dash is louder and more expressive.
How to Type an En Dash

Since it's not on a standard keyboard, here's how to insert it:

  • Mac: Press Option + hyphen (the - key)
  • Windows: Hold Alt and type 0150 on the numeric keypad (not the number row)
  • Microsoft Word / Google Docs: Many word processors automatically convert a hyphen to an en dash when you type a number, then a hyphen, then another number (e.g., typing 10-25 may auto-correct to 10–25)
  • Anywhere: You can copy–paste the character itself: –
Quick Summary

The en dash (–) is a medium-length horizontal punctuation mark. Its job is to connect two things that form a range (pages, dates, times, numbers) or to link two separate but equally weighted things (cities, opposing sides, multi-word modifiers). It means "through," "to," or "between" in a compact visual form. It is longer than a hyphen and shorter than an em dash, and each of those three marks has a distinct role that should not be mixed up.
5201:
En famille means in the company of one's family — doing something with family members, together as a unit, in a private and relaxed home-like setting.

Think of it this way: there are two different versions of almost any gathering — the formal, polished version where outsiders are present, and the warm, comfortable version where it's just family. "En famille" points directly to the second kind.

When something happens en famille, three things are usually true at once:

1. The family is together — the activity is shared by the family as a group, not just one person alone, and not with strangers or the general public.

2. The atmosphere is informal — because it's just family, there's no pressure to perform, dress up, or be guarded. The setting is domestic, relaxed, and intimate. Think of Sunday lunch at home, not a formal dinner with guests.

3. It's private — the family circle is closed. The moment belongs to them alone, away from public life or social obligations.

These three qualities — togetherness, informality, and privacy — are all bundled into this single word. That's what makes it useful: it captures an entire atmosphere in one phrase.
How it works as an adverb

As an adverb, it modifies a verb. It answers the question "in what setting?" or "how?" for whatever action is being described.

It typically appears after the verb or at the end of a sentence:

  • "They dined en famille." → How did they dine? As a family, informally, just among themselves — not at a restaurant or at a formal dinner party.
  • "The evening was spent en famille." → The evening passed in the private, intimate company of the family.

"The president spent the weekend en famille."
He stepped away from his public role and spent the weekend privately, with his family — no aides, no events, just the domestic quiet of family life.

"Christmas was celebrated en famille."
Christmas was not a large gathering with friends, colleagues, or extended guests. It was a quiet, intimate celebration — just the family, the way families do it when it's truly their own.

"She preferred her evenings en famille."
She chose the private warmth of family company over going out socially. The evenings were relaxed, home-centered, shared with the people closest to her.

"The meal, served en famille, had none of the stiffness of a formal dinner."
The meal had a home-style, family-table quality — informal, unguarded, comfortable.

"En famille" has a warm, slightly literary quality. It is used more often in formal writing — journalism, literature, elegant prose — than in everyday casual speech. If someone uses it, they are deliberately evoking a sense of:

  • Coziness and intimacy — the particular comfort that only comes with family
  • Withdrawal from public life — stepping behind a private door, away from the world
  • Unhurried togetherness — time that belongs to the family, not to schedules or obligations

It carries a gentle, old-world elegance — a way of elevating the ordinary act of being with family into something worth naming precisely.

"En famille" does not simply mean informally. Informality is a byproduct of being with family, not the meaning itself. The family presence is the heart of the word. You could have an informal dinner with close friends, but that would not be en famille — because family is not just a mood or an atmosphere. It is the actual people.

Occasionally, writers use it loosely to describe a very close, inseparable group of colleagues or friends who function like a family — but this is a deliberate extension of the original meaning, not the standard use. Whenever you encounter it, the safe and accurate reading is always: with one's family, in a private and relaxed domestic setting.
En famille = doing something in the intimate, private company of one's family, in a relaxed, informal, home-like atmosphere — as a unit, away from the public world.
5202:
"En masse" is a French phrase that English borrowed and made its own. In French, "en" means "in" and "masse" means "mass" or "body" (as in a large group of things gathered together). So literally, it means "in a mass" or "in a body."

You will find this phrase in English writing as far back as the early 1800s. Today, it is so common in English that most people don't even think of it as foreign anymore — it belongs to everyday English.

Say it like this: "on MASS" (the "en" sounds like the French nasal vowel, similar to "on"). In casual American English, many people simply say "en MASS" (rhyming with "in class"), and that is perfectly acceptable.

"En masse" means all together, as one large group, at the same time.

The three key ideas packed inside this phrase are:

1. Large in number. It's not two or three people. It suggests a significant, notable crowd or collection.

2. Together, not separately. This is the heart of the phrase. People (or things) aren't doing something one by one, over different times, or in scattered ways — they are doing it as one unified group.

3. All at once. The action happens simultaneously, not gradually and individually spread out over time.

Think of it this way: imagine a thousand birds sitting on a wire. If they fly away one by one over an hour, that is NOT "en masse." But if they all take off together at the exact same moment in one enormous, sweeping cloud — that is "en masse."
How It Works in a Sentence

"En masse" works as an adverb — meaning it describes how an action is done. You usually place it right after the verb or at the end of the sentence.

Here are clear examples:

  • "The workers resigned en masse."
    → All the workers quit together, at the same time, as a group — not one by one over weeks.
  • "Fans flooded the streets en masse to celebrate the victory."
    → Huge crowds of fans all came out together, all at once.
  • "The emails were deleted en masse."
    → All the emails were wiped out in one sweep, not individually.
  • "Citizens marched en masse to the parliament building to protest."
    → A large group marched together, collectively, as one body.

Notice that "en masse" almost always goes after the action word (verb), not before it. You'd say "they resigned en masse," not "they en masse resigned" (though the latter occasionally appears in literary writing).

"En masse" is not just a fancy way of saying "many people." The emphasis is on the collective, unified nature of the action. It suggests that the group is acting as one force rather than as a bunch of separate individuals who happen to want the same thing.

Compare these two sentences:

  • "Over the years, many employees left the company." — They left separately, at different times. No "en masse" feeling here.
  • "After the scandal, employees left the company en masse." — They all walked out together, around the same time, as a collective reaction. This is "en masse."

The phrase often carries a sense of drama or impact. When something happens en masse, it tends to be striking, hard to ignore, and powerful precisely because it is collective.
Can It Be Used for Things, Not Just People?

Yes! While "en masse" is most commonly associated with people, it works perfectly fine for objects, files, emails, animals, or anything else that can be grouped.

  • "The old records were destroyed en masse."
  • "The company sent the notices en masse."
  • "Birds migrated en masse to warmer climates."
Where You'll Commonly See It Used

"En masse" tends to appear in situations involving collective human behavior, especially dramatic or notable group actions:

  • Protests and demonstrations — People marching or gathering en masse.
  • Resignations — Employees or officials quitting en masse is a very common phrase you'll read in news articles.
  • Migrations or evacuations — Populations fleeing en masse.
  • Purchases or adoptions — Consumers buying a new product en masse, or people adopting a new technology en masse.
  • Deletions or bans — Accounts removed or content deleted en masse.
  • Arrivals — Tourists descending on a place en masse.

• "In droves" — Means in large numbers, often with a sense of a steady, flowing stream. "People left in droves" suggests a continuous outflow. "En masse" is more sudden and simultaneous.
  • "All at once" — A simple, informal way to say the same thing. "En masse" is more formal and more specifically emphasizes the group identity.
  • "Collectively" — Means as a group, but is a bit colder and more neutral. "En masse" is more vivid and carries a sense of scale.
  • "In bulk" — Usually used for goods and products being bought or sold in large quantities. Not used for people.
  • "In a body" — An older, slightly formal English equivalent meaning exactly the same thing as "en masse." Rarely used today.
A Small Note on Writing Style

In formal or academic writing, foreign phrases are traditionally written in italics (en masse). However, because "en masse" has been absorbed so deeply into English, many modern style guides now accept it written in plain Roman text (en masse), without italics. Both are correct — follow the style guide of wherever you are writing, or simply go with italics when in doubt.

If you ever forget everything else, just remember this:

"En masse" = as one large group, all together, all at the same time.

That's the soul of the phrase. Everything else is just detail layered on top of that core idea.
5203:
"En passant" is a French phrase. In French, "en" means "in" or "while," and "passant" comes from the verb passer, meaning "to pass." So the full phrase means "in passing" — as in, something that happens while you are moving past something else.

In everyday language — both in French and occasionally in English — the phrase is used to describe something done casually or incidentally, almost as a side note. If someone says, "I mentioned it en passant," they mean they brought it up briefly, almost offhandedly, without dwelling on it.

However, by far the most famous use of "en passant" is in chess, where it names a very specific, unique, and often misunderstood move. That chess meaning is what most people are referring to when they use this term, and it is the focus of this explanation.

The Foundation: How Pawns Normally Move

To understand en passant, you first need to understand how pawns behave in chess.

A pawn is the smallest and most numerous piece on the board. Each player starts with eight of them. Pawns move forward only, one square at a time. They attack and capture differently from how they move: rather than capturing straight ahead, they capture diagonally — one square to the front-left or front-right.

There is one important exception to the "one square at a time" rule. On a pawn's very first move in the game — and only its first move — it has the option to advance two squares forward instead of one. This is a choice, not a requirement. The player can still move just one square if they prefer.

This two-square option was designed to make chess more dynamic and speed up the opening phase of the game. Without it, pawns would march toward each other very slowly.

The Problem That Made En Passant Necessary

Here's the dilemma this two-square option can create.

Imagine your pawn has advanced deep into your opponent's side of the board — specifically to the fifth row (or "rank") of the board. This is a strong position. Now, your opponent has a pawn sitting on its starting square in the very next column over, right where your pawn could threaten it.

Your opponent uses the two-square first move to slide that pawn forward — jumping right over the square where your pawn could have captured it — and lands safely beside your pawn. In one move, the opponent's pawn has snuck past the danger zone as though your pawn wasn't even there.

This felt deeply unfair to chess players of centuries past. If the opponent's pawn had moved just one square, your pawn could have captured it diagonally. The two-square jump was used to dodge that capture entirely.

En passant was invented to fix this. It says: you may still capture that pawn, even though it has already passed the square where you normally could have taken it. But this right comes with strict conditions.

The Exact Conditions for En Passant

Three specific things must all be true at the same time for en passant to be a legal move.

First, your pawn must be on the fifth rank. The chessboard has eight rows, numbered 1 through 8. White's pawns start on rank 2 and advance toward rank 8; Black's pawns start on rank 7 and advance toward rank 1. For en passant to be possible, your pawn must have already made it to rank 5 (for White) or rank 4 (for Black). This is the midpoint of the board, firmly in the opponent's half.

Second, the opponent's pawn must use its two-square first move and land directly beside yours. The opponent's pawn must travel from its starting square all the way to rank 5 (for Black's pawn) or rank 4 (for White's pawn) in a single move — and it must land in the column immediately to the left or right of your pawn. They must now be standing side by side.

Third, and most critically, you must capture immediately — on your very next turn and no other. The right to capture en passant does not last. The moment the opponent's pawn makes that two-square jump, you have exactly one turn to respond. If you make any other move first, the opportunity disappears forever for that situation. This rule is absolute and has no exceptions.

How the Capture Actually Works

This is the part that makes en passant genuinely strange and unlike any other move in chess: the pawn you capture is not on the square your pawn moves to.

When you execute an en passant capture, your pawn moves diagonally forward — exactly as it would in any normal pawn capture. But instead of landing on the square where the enemy pawn is currently sitting, it lands on the square behind the enemy pawn — the square the opponent's pawn flew over during its two-square jump. That square is empty.

The enemy pawn — still sitting beside your pawn on the rank where it landed — is then simply removed from the board, even though your pawn didn't go there.

This makes en passant the only move in the entire game of chess where a piece captures something that is not on the square it moves to. Every other capture in chess involves a piece landing on the same square that the captured piece occupied. En passant breaks that rule, which is part of why it surprises beginners so often.

A Step-by-Step Example

Let's trace through a concrete example.

White has a pawn on e5 — column e, row 5. Black still has a pawn on d7 — column d, row 7, its original starting square, untouched.

Black decides to use the two-square move and pushes from d7 all the way to d5 in a single turn. Black's pawn now sits on d5, right next to White's pawn on e5. They are side by side.

White now has the en passant option. On White's very next move, White's pawn travels diagonally from e5 to d6 — the square Black's pawn skipped over. Black's pawn, which is sitting on d5 (not d6), is captured and removed from the board. The square White's pawn landed on (d6) was empty the whole time.

If White plays a different move instead — perhaps moving a piece somewhere else — Black's pawn on d5 is now completely safe from en passant. That moment has passed, and it will not come back.

Why En Passant Matters in a Real Game

En passant is not just a rare technicality to mention at dinner parties. It is a genuine tactical tool that shapes real games.

Capturing en passant can shatter an opponent's pawn structure — the arrangement of pawns that determines long-term strength and control of the board. It can open columns and diagonals for your other pieces to become more active. It can relieve pressure in cramped positions. Missing an opponent's en passant threat — or failing to spot your own opportunity — can shift the balance of a game meaningfully.

Importantly, just because you can capture en passant does not always mean you should. The option is a right, not an obligation. Sometimes it is better to leave the pawns as they are and use your turn for something else. Good players weigh this every time the situation arises.

The History: Why This Rule Exists at All

Pawns have not always had the two-square first move. In the earliest forms of chess, every pawn moved only one square at a time, without exception. The two-square option was introduced in Europe around the late 15th century, intended to make games start faster and with more immediate conflict.

But as soon as that rule was introduced, players noticed the problem described above — the two-square move could be used to sneak past an enemy pawn that had already advanced to threaten it. The en passant rule was introduced alongside the two-square move as a corrective measure, ensuring the new option couldn't be abused to bypass a pawn that legitimately threatened capture.

The name perfectly captures the situation. The opponent's pawn passed through a dangerous square. En passant — "in passing" — lets you punish that passage, even after the fact.

Putting It All Together

"En passant" literally means "in passing" in French, and in everyday language describes something done incidentally or as a casual aside. In chess, it is a special pawn capture rule triggered when an opponent uses the two-square first move to bypass a pawn that could have captured it. Your pawn — on the fifth rank — captures by moving to the square the enemy pawn skipped over, and the enemy pawn disappears from the square beside yours. The capture must happen immediately on the very next turn, or the right to it is lost forever. It is the only move in chess where a piece captures something not on the square it lands on, which makes it unique in the game's history and rules.
5204:
"En route" simply means "on the way" or "in the process of traveling to a place."

It describes the moment when a journey has already started but has not yet finished. You have left point A, you haven't reached point B yet, and you are somewhere in between — that is when you are en route.

Think of it like this:

You leave your house to go to school. You are now walking, driving, or riding a bus. You haven't arrived at school yet. At this exact moment, you are en route to school.

"En route" is a French expression that English borrowed and kept exactly as-is. This is why it looks and sounds a little different from typical English words.

In French:

  • "En" means "on" or "in."
  • "Route" means "road" or "way."

So put together, "en route" literally means "on the road" or "on the way." Over time, English speakers adopted it because it was elegant and concise — two little words that perfectly capture the idea of being mid-journey.

This is one of the trickiest things about this expression for learners, because its spelling is French but most English speakers pronounce it in an anglicized way.

The most widely accepted English pronunciation is:

"on ROOT"

You may also hear "on ROWT" (especially in American English), and that is perfectly acceptable too. Both are correct in everyday English.

What you should avoid is pronouncing the "en" like the English letter N on its own, or pronouncing "route" as "rowt-ay" (that would be going too French). Just say "on root" and you will be clearly understood everywhere.
How Is It Used in a Sentence?

"En route" works as an adverb (it describes an action, specifically the action of traveling). It almost always answers the question: "Where is someone or something right now in terms of a journey?"

It is most commonly used in one of two patterns:

Pattern 1: "en route to [destination]"
This tells us both that a journey is in progress AND where the person is heading.

  • "She is en route to the hospital." → She has left, she is traveling, she hasn't arrived yet.
  • "The president is en route to Paris for the summit."
  • "Your pizza is en route to your address."

Pattern 2: "en route" alone (without a destination)
Sometimes the destination is already known from context, so it isn't repeated.

  • "Don't worry, the ambulance is en route." → It's on its way (to you).
  • "The package is en route." → It's being delivered.

Pattern 3: Something happening during the journey
This is a very useful and common way to use it. It means "while on the way to somewhere."

  • "En route to work, he stopped to buy a coffee." → He was traveling to work, and along the way, he stopped for coffee.
  • "They picked up supplies en route to the campsite."
  • "She called me en route to the airport."

Notice in Pattern 3, "en route" can come at the beginning or in the middle of a sentence — both are grammatically correct.

It's worth being precise here, because "en route" has boundaries:

  • It does not mean someone has arrived. The moment they arrive, they are no longer "en route."
  • It does not mean someone is about to leave. If someone is still sitting at home packing their bags, they are not en route yet.
  • It is specifically about active, ongoing travel — the in-between stage.
Can It Be Used for Non-Physical Journeys?

Yes, but only in a loose, informal sense. You might occasionally hear things like:

  • "She is en route to becoming a doctor" — meaning she is in the process of achieving it, not there yet.

However, this is a metaphorical stretch. The expression is most naturally and most correctly used for actual, physical travel. Stick to that meaning and you will never go wrong.

This is important. The correct spelling is always two separate words:

✅ en route

You may sometimes see "enroute" (one word) written informally, especially in American English. While this shows up occasionally, it is not considered standard or correct in formal writing. Always write it as two words unless a specific style guide you are following says otherwise.

A hyphen ("en-route") is also sometimes seen, but again, the cleanest and most universally accepted spelling is the two-word version: en route.

MeaningOn the way; in the middle of a journey
OriginFrench — "on the road"
Pronunciation"on ROOT"
SpellingAlways two words: en route
Used whenA journey has started but not finished
Common pattern"en route to [place]"
One Final Way to Remember It Forever

Picture a delivery truck. It has left the warehouse. It hasn't reached your door yet. It is somewhere on the roads between those two points. The tracking app says: "Your order is en route."

That image — something or someone in motion, between start and finish — is the heart of "en route." Whenever you use this expression, that is exactly what you are describing.
5205:
Enact means to make something real and official through a deliberate, authoritative action. It is about taking something that exists as an idea, a plan, or a proposal — and bringing it into formal existence.

The word has two distinct but related senses. Understanding both will give you complete command of it.
Sense 1: To Pass Something as a Law

This is the most common and important use of "enact." When a government body — a parliament, a congress, a legislature — officially passes a bill and turns it into law, they enact it.

Think of it this way: a bill is just a proposal sitting on paper. The moment the authorities officially approve it and give it legal force, it becomes law — and that process of converting proposal into law is called enacting.

Examples:

  • The government enacted a law requiring all drivers to wear seatbelts.
  • Parliament enacted new regulations to reduce air pollution.
  • The bill was enacted after years of debate.

Key point: Enact in this sense carries a sense of formal authority. It's not just agreeing on something casually — it involves an official institution using its power to make something legally binding.
Sense 2: To Perform or Act Something Out

The second sense of "enact" means to perform, portray, or play out a story, a role, a scene, or an event — especially in a deliberate and vivid way. When you enact something, you are not just describing it; you are actively bringing it to life through performance or action.

Examples:

  • The students enacted the story of Romeo and Juliet on stage.
  • The soldiers re-enacted the famous battle for a history documentary.
  • She enacted the role of a fearless warrior with great conviction.

Key point: Enact in this sense suggests that the performance is purposeful and deliberate — done with care and intent, not casually or accidentally.

Though these two meanings seem different on the surface, they share a common thread: deliberate, intentional action that gives something concrete form. Whether you are turning a bill into law or bringing a story to life on stage, you are taking something that was previously abstract and making it real and active.

You might wonder — why not just say "do" or "perform" instead of "enact"?

The difference is that enact carries a weight of formality, authority, and deliberateness that those simpler words do not. Saying "the government did a law" sounds weak and informal. Saying "the government enacted a law" sounds precise and powerful. Similarly, "the children performed a scene" is fine, but "the children enacted a scene" suggests they played it out in a vivid, true-to-life way.

Use "enact" when you want to convey that the action was official, intentional, and carried real significance.

• Enactment (noun) — the process of enacting something, or the law/rule that was enacted. "The enactment of the new policy took three years."
  • Re-enact (verb) — to enact again; to repeat or recreate an event or performance. "Historians re-enacted the signing of the declaration."
  • Re-enactment (noun) — a recreation of a past event. "The battle re-enactment drew a large crowd."

In the legal sense: pass, legislate, institute, establish, decree, ratify, establish, ordain.

In the performance sense: perform, act out, portray, play out, depict, stage, represent.

In the legal sense, the opposite of enacting a law is repealing it (canceling or removing it). Other opposites include: revoke, annul, abolish, overturn.

In the performance sense, there is no single direct opposite, but you might say something is omitted, skipped, or simply not performed.

SenseWhat it meansExample

To put it plainly:

  • If a government enacts something → they officially make it a law.
  • If a person or group enacts something → they bring it to life through performance.

In both cases, enact means taking something from the world of ideas and making it real, official, and active through purposeful, deliberate action.
5206: "Enamel" always refers to a very hard, smooth, glass-like coating or material — something that forms a tough outer layer to protect what's underneath and often looks shiny or glossy. Whether you're talking about teeth, pots, or jewelry, this core idea of a hard, glassy surface is always present.

1. The Hard Coating on Your Teeth

This is probably the most common use of the word in everyday life.

When people say "tooth enamel" or just "enamel," they mean the outermost layer of a tooth — the visible white part that covers the crown (the part of the tooth above the gum line). It acts like a protective shell over the softer inner layers of the tooth.

Enamel is actually the hardest substance the human body produces — harder than bone. It's made almost entirely of tightly packed mineral crystals, which is what gives it that extreme hardness. This toughness allows it to handle the enormous pressure of biting and chewing thousands of times every day.

However, despite being so hard, enamel has a critical weakness: it cannot repair itself. Unlike a broken bone, which can heal, enamel has no living cells once your tooth fully forms. This is why dentists warn you to protect it. Acids — from sugary foods, fizzy drinks, fruit juices, or the bacteria in your mouth — can gradually dissolve and erode enamel in a process called demineralisation. Once it's gone, it's gone forever.

This is the reason behind dental advice like: don't sip on acidic drinks all day, wait before brushing after eating, use fluoride toothpaste. Fluoride actually helps by strengthening enamel's mineral structure. Thin or damaged enamel leads to sensitive teeth (you feel pain when eating hot, cold, or sweet things) because the inner, more sensitive layer of the tooth becomes exposed.

2. A Glassy Coating Fused onto Metal or Ceramics

This is the oldest use of the word, and it refers to a completely different material — not biological at all.

In this sense, enamel is a hard, glassy coating that is applied to the surface of metal, ceramic, or glass and then permanently fused to it by heating at very high temperatures. The result is a smooth, durable, often colourful layer that is bonded tightly to the object beneath it.

Here's how it works in simple terms: powdered glass (often mixed with colouring pigments) is applied to a metal surface and then placed inside a very hot furnace or kiln. The heat causes the glass powder to melt, flow over the surface, and then harden as it cools — permanently fusing itself to the metal. The final surface looks and feels glassy: smooth, shiny, and slightly reflective.

This type of enamel goes by several names:

  • Vitreous enamel (vitreous means "glass-like")
  • Porcelain enamel
  • Fired enamel

Where you encounter it:

  • Cookware — Enamel-coated pots and pans (like the famous Le Creuset cast iron pots) have a white or coloured glassy interior. The enamel makes them non-reactive (so acidic food doesn't interact with the metal), easy to clean, and resistant to rust and corrosion.
  • Bathtubs and sinks — Many classic bathtubs are made of cast iron with a white enamel coating. That's what gives them their smooth, bright-white, easy-to-clean surface.
  • Household appliances — The interiors of many ovens are coated in enamel for easy cleaning.
  • Street signs and vintage advertisement signs — Outdoor signs used enamel coating because it doesn't fade in sunlight, doesn't rust, and is extremely durable. Old train station signs and vintage shop signs were often made this way.
  • Mugs and cups — Traditional camping mugs (those slightly speckled metal cups) are enamelware — metal coated with enamel.

Key properties of this kind of enamel:

  • Very hard and scratch-resistant (though it can chip if knocked sharply)
  • Non-porous — liquids and bacteria can't seep into it
  • Heat-resistant
  • Chemically inert — it doesn't react with food or cleaning agents
  • Can be made in any colour
  • Smooth and glossy surface

3. Decorative Enamel in Art and Jewellery

This is an extension of the same glass-fused-onto-metal idea, but used as an art form. Decorative enamel involves applying coloured glassy enamel to jewellery, decorative objects, religious artefacts, and ornamental items — essentially painting with glass that is then fired permanently onto the piece.

This art form is ancient. Enamel jewellery and decorative objects have been found from ancient Egypt, ancient Greece, and Byzantine civilisation. Today, it is still used in fine jewellery, medals, badges, and luxury watches.

There are a few famous techniques used in decorative enamel work:

  • Cloisonné (klwah-zo-nay): Thin metal wires are bent into patterns and soldered onto a metal base, creating tiny compartments (called cloisons, meaning "cells" in French). Each compartment is then filled with a different colour of powdered enamel paste and fired. The result is a brilliantly coloured, intricately patterned surface. Chinese cloisonné is particularly famous.
  • Champlevé (sham-luh-vay): Instead of wire walls, shallow recesses or channels are carved directly into the metal surface. These carved spaces are filled with enamel paste and fired. The metal surface between the filled areas remains visible.
  • Plique-à-jour (pleek-ah-zhoor): Perhaps the most delicate technique — enamel is applied within a framework with no metal backing, so light shines through the coloured glass. The effect looks like a miniature stained-glass window.

In all these techniques, "enamel" refers to the coloured glass material that is fused into place by heat.

4. Enamel Paint

"Enamel" is also used as the name for a specific type of paint that dries to an especially hard, smooth, and glossy finish — one that resembles the glassy quality of vitreous enamel. The name is borrowed because the dried result looks and behaves somewhat like true fired enamel: it's hard, shiny, and durable.

Enamel paint (unlike gloss or matt emulsion paint) creates a surface that is tougher and more resistant to knocks, moisture, and cleaning. This makes it ideal for surfaces that take a lot of wear or need frequent wiping:

  • Kitchen and bathroom walls and woodwork
  • Furniture
  • Metal railings and gates
  • Floor surfaces
  • Cabinets and shelving

It's important to know that modern enamel paint does not actually contain glass or go through a firing process. It's simply a hard, oil- or water-based paint. The word "enamel" in this context is used more loosely — it describes the quality of the dried surface (hard, smooth, glossy) rather than its actual composition. True vitreous enamel and enamel paint are very different things technically; they just share a name because of that surface similarity.

5. Nail Enamel

"Nail enamel" is simply another word for nail polish or nail varnish — the coloured coating applied to fingernails and toenails for decoration and minor protection. The word "enamel" is used here because nail polish, like vitreous enamel, forms a hard, smooth, glossy, coloured coating over a surface. High-end brands often prefer the term "nail enamel" as it sounds more refined than "nail polish."

Now that you've seen all the different uses, notice what they all share:

SenseWhat it isKey quality

Actually, let me put it in words: every use of "enamel" involves something that is hard, smooth, and glass-like — whether that's the mineral coating on your teeth, the fired glass on your cookware, the decorative glass in jewellery, or the glossy dried layer of a special paint. The word carries a consistent underlying idea: a tough, protective, polished surface that resists damage and looks clean and glossy.

• On teeth: The hard, white mineral outer layer of a tooth. Hardest thing in the body. Cannot regenerate. Attacked by acid.
  • On objects (fired/vitreous enamel): A glassy coating fused onto metal or ceramic by heat. Used on cookware, bathtubs, signs, mugs. Hard, colourful, non-reactive, durable.
  • In art/jewellery: The same glassy material used decoratively — fired into metal compartments or carvings to create coloured designs.
  • As paint: A hard, glossy paint that mimics the smooth, tough quality of fired enamel. Used on surfaces needing durability.
  • On nails: Another word for nail polish — a coloured coating that dries hard and shiny.

In all cases: hard + smooth + glassy + protective = enamel.

To enamor someone means to fill them with a strong feeling of love, admiration, or deep fascination toward a person or a thing. When someone is enamored, they are not just casually interested — they are genuinely charmed, captivated, and deeply drawn to whatever has caught their attention.

Think of it this way: if something enamors you, it grabs hold of your heart and mind so strongly that you can't help but love it or be fascinated by it.

This word covers two broad situations:

1. Romantic love toward a person
Someone can be enamored of another person — meaning they are deeply attracted to them, often in a loving or smitten way.

"He was completely enamored of her — he thought about her all day."

2. Strong admiration or passion for a thing
Someone can also be enamored of an idea, a place, an art form, a subject — anything that deeply fascinates or delights them. This use has nothing romantic about it. It simply means a powerful fondness or passion.

"She became enamored with jazz after hearing it for the first time."
"The young student was enamored of philosophy and read everything he could find."

So the word works both in the romantic sense and in the broader sense of being powerfully drawn to or passionate about something.

This is important, because enamor is almost always used in the passive voice in real life. You will rarely see someone say "Paris enamored him" (active). Instead, people almost always say:

  • "He was enamored of Paris."
  • "She was enamored with the idea."
  • "They were enamored by his performance."

All three prepositions — of, with, and by — are commonly used after "enamored." None of them is wrong. "Enamored of" is the most classic and formal-sounding. "Enamored with" is the most common in everyday modern English.

The feeling described by "enamored" sits at the deeper end of the spectrum — well beyond casual liking or simple interest.

Think of it on a scale:

Notice → Like → Admire → Be Enamored Of → Obsess Over

Being enamored is a genuine, meaningful level of love or fascination. It is not as extreme or uncontrolled as obsession, but it is much stronger than merely "liking" or "being interested in" something.

One very common and important use of this word is the negative form — saying someone is not enamored of something. This is a polite, slightly understated way of saying someone is unimpressed, unenthusiastic, or simply doesn't like something.

"The manager was not enamored with the new plan." (= She didn't like it.)
"He was not exactly enamored of the idea of working overtime." (= He was quite against it.)

This negative use is extremely natural in English, especially in written or formal contexts, so it is worth remembering.

• American English: enamor
  • British English: enamour

Both mean exactly the same thing. The only difference is spelling based on regional convention.

ContextExample
Romantic"He was enamored with her from the moment they met."
Travel"Visitors quickly become enamored with the city's beauty."
Art / Music"She was enamored of classical Indian music."
Ideas"The philosopher was enamored with the concept of freedom."
Nature"As a child, he was enamored by the ocean."
Negative use"She was not enamored with the new office rules."
How It Differs From Similar Words

Several words are close to "enamored" in meaning, but each has a slightly different shade:

  • Smitten — very similar, but almost always romantic, and suggests the feeling hit suddenly, like a bolt. More informal and playful in tone.
  • Infatuated — suggests an intense but somewhat irrational or short-lived attraction. It carries a slight hint that the feeling may not be based on reality or good judgment.
  • Captivated — means held completely by something fascinating, but is more about attention and interest than love or deep passion.
  • Charmed — a lighter, warmer word, suggesting delight rather than deep passion.
  • Enchanted — has a magical, dreamy quality to it.

Enamored is more balanced and neutral than all of these. It suggests genuine, heartfelt love or admiration without implying irrationality (like infatuation) or sudden impact (like smitten). It also works across both romantic and non-romantic situations, which makes it more versatile.

"Enamored" is a slightly formal, literary word. You will find it more often in writing — books, articles, reviews, and formal speech — than in casual everyday conversation. That said, it is not rare or difficult-sounding. It is a perfectly natural word that educated speakers use regularly.

If you said it in conversation, it would sound thoughtful and articulate, not stuffy.

To enamor = to cause someone to feel strong love, admiration, or deep fascination toward a person or thing.
Most commonly used as: "be enamored of / with / by" something.
Works for romantic love and non-romantic passion or admiration.
The negative form ("not enamored with") is very common and means unimpressed or unenthusiastic.
Slightly formal in tone, versatile in use.
5208:
To be enamored means to be filled with a deep, powerful feeling of love, admiration, or fascination — toward a person, a thing, or even an idea. It goes far beyond simply liking something. When you are enamored, you are captivated. You can't stop thinking about it. It holds a special, almost magical place in your heart or mind.

Think of it as the feeling when something or someone grabs hold of you so strongly that you are pulled toward it with warmth and excitement.

The word works in two related but distinct situations:

1. Romantic love
This is the more traditional use. Being enamored with a person means you are deeply, intensely attracted to them — you are smitten, enchanted, in love. It carries a sense of being under a spell.

He was completely enamored with her — he thought about her all day and smiled every time her name came up.

2. Strong admiration or fascination (non-romantic)
This is just as common and important. You can be enamored with a place, a hobby, an idea, a book, a city, a sport — anything. It means you find it deeply appealing, you are drawn to it, and you enjoy or admire it greatly.

She became enamored with painting after her first art class — she bought brushes that same evening.
The tourists were enamored with the city's old streets and colorful markets.
He has always been enamored with the idea of traveling the world alone.

This is important: enamored is not a mild word. It sits well above "interested" or "fond of." Here is a rough ladder to show you where it stands:

  • Slightly interested → fond of → in love with / fascinated by → enamored → obsessed

Enamored sits near the top. It suggests a strong, warm, genuine feeling — but it is not yet obsessive or unhealthy. It is deeply positive and enthusiastic.

Here is a nuance that makes the word richer: when someone is enamored, they often see the object of their admiration through rose-colored glasses. They may overlook its flaws or imperfections because they are so charmed by it.

He was so enamored with the old house that he ignored all the cracks in the walls and the leaking roof.

This slight sense of being charmed to the point of not seeing things clearly is built into the word's feeling, even if it isn't always stated directly.

"Enamored" is almost always followed by with or of. Both are correct, though enamored with is more common in American English, and enamored of is more traditional and slightly more formal.

  • She was enamored with the novel.
  • He was enamored of her wit and intelligence.

You will almost never see "enamored" standing alone without one of these prepositions following it.
The Negative Form — and Why It Matters

One highly useful way the word appears is in the negative: not enamored with/of.

When used this way, it is a polite, understated way of saying you dislike something or are unimpressed by it. This is common in formal or professional speech.

The manager was not enamored with the new proposal. (= she didn't like it at all)
I have to say, I'm not particularly enamored with this plan. (= I think this is a poor idea)

Notice how saying "not enamored with" sounds more measured and sophisticated than simply saying "I hate this" or "I don't like this." It is a refined way of expressing disapproval.
The Register: When Do People Use This Word?

"Enamored" is a slightly formal and literary word. You are more likely to encounter it in:

  • Written English (novels, articles, essays)
  • Formal or professional speech
  • Situations where someone wants to sound expressive or eloquent

In everyday casual conversation, people are more likely to say "I'm obsessed with," "I'm in love with," "I'm fascinated by," or simply "I really love" — but all of those can often be replaced by "enamored" when you want a more refined tone.

AspectDetail

Enamored means deeply captivated — by a person (romantically) or by anything else (a place, idea, hobby, work of art) through powerful admiration and fascination. It is stronger than "liking" something. It carries a warm, enchanted quality, sometimes with a hint of being so charmed that you overlook flaws. It is paired with with or of, and in its negative form (not enamored with), it becomes a refined way to express dislike or disapproval. It is a slightly formal word, most at home in writing or thoughtful speech.

Once you know this word, you will start noticing it everywhere — and you may even find yourself becoming a little enamored with it.

To encamp means to settle into a temporary place by setting up a camp. When a group of people stop at a location — pitching tents, arranging their supplies, and preparing to stay for a while — they encamp there. Think of it as the action of making a temporary home out in the open, away from permanent buildings or established settlements.

The key word here is temporary. People who encamp are not moving into a permanent home. They are pausing at a spot, setting up what they need to survive and rest there, and they will eventually move on or be moved.

The verb "encamp" can work in two closely related ways:

1. Without an object (intransitive) — the group itself does the encamping

This is the most common use. The group is the one settling down.

"The soldiers encamped by the river."
"The protesters encamped in the city square for weeks."
"The travelers encamped at the edge of the forest before continuing their journey at dawn."

In these sentences, the soldiers, protesters, and travelers are all doing the action themselves — they stopped, they set up camp, they settled in.

2. With an object (transitive) — someone encamps others somewhere

Here, a person in authority or control is settling a group of people into a camp.

"The general encamped his troops in the valley."
"Aid workers helped encamp the refugees near the border."

In these sentences, one person or group is placing another group into a camp. The general didn't go to the valley himself to set up a tent — he directed his troops to do so and made sure they were settled there.

Once a group has finished encamping, they are described as encamped — this is the past tense, but it also works as a describing word (adjective) to show the state of being settled in a camp.

"By nightfall, the army was encamped along the ridge."
"Thousands of displaced families remained encamped near the border for months."

Being "encamped" suggests the group is currently stationed there, living out of a camp. They have settled in, but it is still temporary.

While encamp can technically apply to anyone setting up a camp, it is most naturally used for:

  • Soldiers and armies — historically the most classic use. Armies on the march would encamp for the night or before a battle.
  • Refugees and displaced people — people forced from their homes who set up temporary shelters somewhere.
  • Protesters and demonstrators — groups who occupy a public space by setting up a visible, sustained camp presence.
  • Explorers and travelers — people on long journeys through wilderness who stop to rest.
  • Rescue or aid workers — teams operating in the field away from cities.
How It Feels as a Word (Register and Tone)

"Encamp" is a formal and somewhat serious word. You would not typically hear it in casual everyday conversation. Instead of saying "Let's encamp here," most people in ordinary speech would say "Let's set up camp here" or "Let's make camp here."

However, you will often see "encamp" in:

  • News reporting (especially on military operations, refugee crises, or protest movements)
  • Historical writing (about wars, expeditions, and ancient armies)
  • Literature (novels and stories set in military or wilderness contexts)
  • Official or governmental language

So when you encounter it in these settings, you can confidently understand that someone — or some group — is establishing a temporary camp at a specific place.

The noun directly born from this verb is encampment. An encampment is the place or site where a group has encamped — the actual camp itself.

"The army's encampment stretched for miles."
"Police moved in to clear the protest encampment."

So: the action of settling into camp = to encamp. The place where they have settled = the encampment.
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

Imagine a large army marching across a country. As evening falls, the general gives the order to stop. The soldiers unpack their gear, pitch their tents, light their fires, and prepare for the night. That entire process — stopping, setting up, and settling in temporarily — is encamping. Once they are all set up and resting, they are encamped. The site where they are staying is their encampment. When morning comes, they will pack up and march again — because encamping is never permanent.

That is the full picture of this word.
